comment_box:
I write in strong support of the Department of Veterans Affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the
long-standing exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the VA medical benefits
package and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs
(CHAMPVA).
This proposed rule restores the VA’s medical services to align with decades of
federal policy, precedent, and ethical healthcare practice and correctly recognizes the statutory limitations
and moral concerns long held by taxpayers and federal lawmakers regarding federal funding of
elective abortion.

For over two decades—from the establishment of the medical benefits package in 1999 until
2022—the VA appropriately interpreted abortion services as not “needed” under 38 U.S.C. §
1710. That position reflected both legal prudence and widespread public sentiment. The Biden
administration created a de facto entitlement for abortion services at federal expense by reversing that understanding in 2022. By so doing, the Biden administration circumvented long-established legal frameworks, ignored state laws, and contradicted the very intent of the Supreme Court’s
decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which returned authority over abortion regulation to the states.

The proposed rule affirms that VA has always covered medically necessary care, including interventions for ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage management, and circumstances where a mother’s life is at risk. The revised language maintains these life-saving exceptions while reinstating the broader prohibition on elective abortion—a line Congress has drawn for decades across multiple federal programs, including Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health
Benefits Program, and TRICARE.

The VA’s authority to define “needed” services under 38 U.S.C. § 1710 is not unlimited and must reflect the legislative and ethical boundaries established by Congress. The rule also restores CHAMPVA coverage to be consistent with TRICARE policy, which restricts abortion funding except when the mother’s life is endangered.

There are no states that prohibits emergency treatment for conditions like ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage. Suggesting otherwise—as the prior administration’s interim final rule did—was incorrect and inflammatory.

This proposed rule reaffirms that the VA’s role is to provide legitimate, life-affirming medical services to veterans and their families—not to serve as an avenue for taxpayer-subsidized elective abortions. 
The Department of Veterans Affairs is to be commended for returning to a policy that respects human life, reflects the legal and moral will of Congress, and ensures that taxpayer resources are used responsibly and ethically.

Stephanie Holden Smith
Alabama Policy Institute 
President/CEO
